claims.text: An optimum Cu or Cu-like element concentration creates a beneficial balance between phase separation and deformation-induced twinning that retains or enhances toughness.
Cu concentrations below the optimum cause insufficient twin-mediated crack bridging and inferior toughness.
Cu concentrations above the optimum cause excessive grain-boundary decohesion and inferior toughness.
Heavy cold drawing of a Co-Cu-Fe-Mn-Ni HEA can produce an ultrafine dual-fcc lamellar microstructure consisting of Co-Fe-rich and Cu-rich phases.
Changing Cu concentration alters the degree of phase separation and deformation-induced twin formation.
Deformation-induced twin boundaries shield crack propagation.
Cu-rich phase-separated regions can act as beneficial twin-nucleation sites.
Cu-rich regions can act as sites of grain-boundary decoupling or decohesion.
Controlled phase separation at optimal Cu content produces fine, well-distributed lamellae that facilitate deformation twinning.
The resulting twin boundaries provide crack bridging and strain partitioning that enhance toughness.
Insufficient Cu produces too little phase separation to activate the proposed twinning mechanism.
Excessive Cu segregation weakens grain-boundary cohesion and promotes early intergranular cracking.
An optimally Cu-doped alloy should have greater fracture toughness than an identically processed baseline with conventional minor Cu content.
An optimally Cu-doped alloy should exhibit higher strain hardening and more uniform deformation than the baseline.
An optimally Cu-doped alloy should exhibit a higher density of deformation-induced twins and less grain-boundary decohesion than the baseline.
Both lower and higher Cu concentrations should produce lower toughness than the intermediate optimum.
The proposed behavior primarily applies to fcc-based or dual-phase HEAs subjected to severe plastic deformation at ambient or moderate temperatures.
The proposed behavior may not apply to single-phase BCC HEAs or alloys processed without significant phase separation.
Fracture toughness can be determined through the proposed standard tensile or bending tests.
